title: Pediatric Respiratory Infections: Severity and Syndrome Before Antibiotics
bottomLine: Most pediatric respiratory infections are viral and supportive-care problems, but age, work of breathing, oxygenation, hydration and focal findings determine who needs testing, antibiotics, imaging or hospital-level care. Diagnose the syndrome before choosing the drug.
recognize: Tachypnea, retractions, grunting, hypoxemia, dehydration and altered interaction are more important severity cues than fever height alone.
Bronchiolitis, viral URI, croup, influenza, pneumonia and asthma can overlap in symptoms but require different management.
differentiate: Diffuse viral wheeze/crackles in an infant differs from focal bacterial pneumonia; croup stridor differs from lower-airway wheeze.
A normal early chest radiograph or modest fever does not override significant respiratory distress.
assessment: Assess age, immunization, respiratory rate/effort, SpO2, hydration, feeding, fever duration, focal auscultatory findings, comorbidity and exposure history.
workup: Use viral testing, chest radiography or microbiology only when the result will change isolation, antiviral, antibiotic, disposition or complication management.
Routine imaging is low value in uncomplicated bronchiolitis or a typical mild viral syndrome.
management: Provide syndrome-appropriate supportive care and treat hypoxemia/dehydration.
Use antibiotics only when bacterial pneumonia or another bacterial syndrome is sufficiently likely and select therapy using current Canadian pediatric guidance and local resistance context.
Escalate severe work of breathing, hypoxemia, apnea, exhaustion or inability to hydrate.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine cough/cold medications in young children and avoid antibiotics for uncomplicated viral illness.
Antiviral decisions for influenza/COVID or high-risk hosts are age-, timing- and risk-specific.
counselling: Teach expected viral course, hydration/fever comfort measures and concrete return precautions for breathing, hydration or behaviour change.
followUp: Reassess when symptoms worsen, fever persists unexpectedly or the child fails to improve on the expected trajectory.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because the child has fever and cough without first deciding whether the syndrome is viral, bacterial, obstructive or upper-airway disease.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric respiratory illness, severity and syndrome come before the prescription.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society respiratory/infectious-disease practice statements
Choosing Wisely Canada pediatric stewardship recommendations

title: Pediatric GI Disorders: Hydration, Obstruction, Inflammation, and Growth
bottomLine: Pediatric GI complaints are triaged by hydration, bilious emesis, bleeding, peritonitis, growth and age-specific obstruction patterns. Do not call persistent vomiting, abdominal pain or diarrhea benign until the child's hydration, growth and surgical red flags are assessed.
recognize: Acute gastroenteritis commonly causes vomiting/diarrhea with dehydration risk; chronic symptoms require growth and inflammatory/malabsorption review.
Age-specific surgical patterns include pyloric stenosis, intussusception, malrotation/volvulus and appendicitis.
differentiate: Bilious vomiting is obstruction until proven otherwise and is not routine reflux/gastroenteritis.
Functional abdominal pain/constipation are diagnoses made in the context of normal growth and absent alarm features.
assessment: Assess hydration, urine output, weight trajectory, vomiting colour, stool blood, fever, pain localization, abdominal distension/peritoneal signs, diet, travel, medications and family history.
workup: Use electrolytes, stool studies, celiac/inflammatory testing or imaging only when severity, duration, age or alarm features justify them.
Choose ultrasound preferentially when it answers appendiceal, pyloric, intussusception or biliary questions without radiation.
management: Use oral rehydration for appropriate mild/moderate dehydration and IV resuscitation when shock, severe dehydration or oral failure is present.
Escalate suspected obstruction, peritonitis, significant GI bleeding, severe inflammatory disease or growth failure.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine antimotility therapy in young children with acute infectious diarrhea.
Antiemetic use, acid suppression and laxatives should be age/indication appropriate rather than reflexive.
counselling: Teach hydration goals, oral-rehydration technique and return precautions for decreased urine, lethargy, blood, bilious emesis or worsening pain.
followUp: Track growth and symptom resolution; chronic/recurrent symptoms need a documented diagnostic plan rather than repeated empiric medications.
examTrap: Calling bilious vomiting gastroenteritis because the child also has diarrhea.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric GI care, bilious vomiting and growth failure change the pathway immediately.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society acute gastroenteritis/rehydration resources
Canadian pediatric surgical and gastroenterology practice principles

title: Pediatric Skin Conditions: Barrier Disease, Infection, and Dangerous Rash
bottomLine: Most childhood rashes are benign or chronic inflammatory disease, but fever/toxicity, pain out of proportion, mucosal involvement, purpura, blistering or rapidly spreading infection require urgent evaluation. Treat the morphology and clinical syndrome, not the colour alone.
recognize: Atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, impetigo, tinea, viral exanthems, insect reactions and acne are common.
Barrier disruption from eczema/abrasion increases bacterial skin-infection risk.
differentiate: Nonpurulent cellulitis differs from drainable abscess; eczema flare differs from eczema herpeticum or secondary bacterial infection.
Non-blanching purpura with systemic illness differs from a benign blanching viral exanthem.
assessment: Describe morphology/distribution, blanching, pain/pruritus, mucosal involvement, fever/systemic status, medication exposure, immune status and recurrence/contact history.
workup: Cultures are selective—use them when purulence, recurrence, treatment failure or unusual host/pathogen risk will change care.
Do not order broad allergy testing for uncomplicated eczema without a specific immediate-type food/allergy history.
management: Use skin-barrier care and appropriate topical therapy for dermatitis; treat bacterial/fungal disease according to morphology/severity.
Drain abscesses when indicated and escalate rapidly progressive, deep, necrotizing or systemic infection.
medicationSafety: Use topical corticosteroid potency/site appropriately and avoid steroid monotherapy for undiagnosed fungal infection.
Antibiotic therapy follows current CPS/local stewardship rather than routine broad MRSA coverage for every lesion.
counselling: Teach barrier care, medication amount/site and signs of superinfection without blaming hygiene.
followUp: Reassess treatment failure, recurrence or atypical morphology and consider dermatology when chronic disease remains poorly controlled.
examTrap: Treating every erythematous rash with antibiotics or assuming a child with fever and non-blanching purpura has a routine viral exanthem.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric skin diagnosis starts with morphology plus how sick the child is.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society 2026 community-associated bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection statement

title: Childhood Fever: Age and Appearance Determine the Pathway
bottomLine: Fever is a sign, not a diagnosis. Age, appearance, immunization, host risk and source determine testing and disposition. A well-appearing febrile young infant ≤90 days follows a dedicated Canadian age-stratified pathway; an ill-appearing child of any age needs immediate stabilization and sepsis-focused assessment.
recognize: Young infants can have serious bacterial infection with subtle findings.
Older immunized children with a clear viral syndrome often need less testing, while immunocompromise or focal red flags broaden evaluation.
differentiate: Response to antipyretics does not distinguish viral from bacterial infection.
Fever without source differs by age: young-infant risk algorithms must not be copied onto older children or vice versa.
assessment: Assess ABCs, perfusion, mental status/interaction, hydration, respiratory effort, rash, neck stiffness, focal source, immune status, immunization and duration.
workup: For well-appearing febrile infants ≤90 days, use current CPS age-stratified urine/blood/CSF/inflammatory-marker guidance.
For older children, test according to source/risk; avoid indiscriminate CBC/culture/imaging in a well child with a clear uncomplicated viral syndrome.
management: Stabilize and treat suspected sepsis/meningitis promptly.
Use age/risk appropriate empiric antibiotics only when indicated and provide close follow-up/return precautions for outpatient pathways.
medicationSafety: Antipyretics improve comfort but do not prevent serious bacterial disease; dose by current weight and avoid unsafe combination/dosing practices.
counselling: Teach caregivers to focus on breathing, hydration, arousal and evolving symptoms—not fever number alone.
followUp: Ensure reliable follow-up for selected outpatient young-infant pathways and reassess persistent fever or evolving focal symptoms.
examTrap: Discharging a well-looking 6-week-old with fever using the same low-risk reasoning used for a healthy 5-year-old.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric fever risk is age plus appearance plus host context—not temperature alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society — Management of well-appearing febrile young infants aged ≤90 days, updated 2026

title: Acute Otitis Media: Diagnose the Middle Ear Before Prescribing
bottomLine: Acute otitis media requires acute symptoms plus objective middle-ear inflammation/effusion. A red tympanic membrane alone—especially in a crying child—does not establish AOM. Use observation selectively in appropriate nonsevere disease and antibiotics when age/severity/diagnostic certainty warrant them.
recognize: Bulging tympanic membrane and middle-ear effusion with compatible acute symptoms are more diagnostic than erythema alone.
Otitis media with effusion lacks acute bacterial symptoms and usually does not need antibiotics.
differentiate: Otitis externa causes canal pain/inflammation; referred dental/pharyngeal pain can mimic ear disease.
Mastoid tenderness/swelling or cranial complications are not uncomplicated AOM.
assessment: Assess age, pain/fever, duration, bilateral disease, otorrhea, recurrence, immune/craniofacial risk and examine both tympanic membranes with adequate visualization.
workup: No routine labs/imaging are required for uncomplicated AOM; culture/imaging is for treatment failure or complications.
management: Use watchful waiting with reliable follow-up for selected mild cases and current CPS first-line antibiotic guidance when treatment is indicated.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated broad-spectrum antibiotics without confirming diagnosis or treatment failure.
Duration is age/severity specific; do not apply one duration to every child.
redFlags: Persistent severe symptoms despite appropriate therapy
counselling: Explain why pain control matters even when antibiotics are prescribed and why effusion/hearing symptoms can persist after acute infection resolves.
followUp: Reassess treatment failure and persistent effusion with hearing/language impact.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for a red tympanic membrane without bulging/effusion or compatible acute disease.
oneLinePearl: AOM is a middle-ear diagnosis, not a colour diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society — Management of acute otitis media in children six months and older, reaffirmed 2024

title: Pediatric Pharyngitis: Test the Right Child, Treat Confirmed GAS
bottomLine: Most sore throats are viral. Use age and clinical features to decide who needs GAS testing; cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness or oral ulcers make GAS less likely. Treat confirmed GAS to prevent complications, but do not prescribe antibiotics from throat appearance alone.
recognize: GAS more often causes acute sore throat, fever, tender anterior cervical nodes, tonsillar inflammation/exudate and absence of prominent viral features.
differentiate: Viral pharyngitis, EBV, peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess and epiglottic/deep-neck disease require different evaluation.
A positive test in a child with strong viral features can represent carriage rather than the cause of symptoms.
assessment: Assess age, viral features, neck swelling, trismus, muffled voice, drooling, airway symptoms, rash, splenomegaly and community/household risk.
workup: Use rapid antigen/molecular or throat culture according to the current Canadian testing pathway when GAS probability justifies testing.
Do not routinely swab children with clear viral pharyngitis.
management: Treat confirmed GAS with guideline-concordant therapy and evaluate deep-space/airway complications urgently.
Support hydration and analgesia for viral illness.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for uncomplicated pharyngitis.
If EBV is plausible, interpret aminopenicillin-associated rash appropriately rather than automatically labelling lifelong penicillin allergy.
counselling: Explain why testing prevents both unnecessary antibiotics and missed GAS when clinically appropriate.
followUp: Reassess persistent/worsening symptoms or concern for abscess/complication; routine test-of-cure is not needed after uncomplicated successfully treated GAS.
examTrap: Swabbing and treating every sore throat despite cough, rhinorrhea and hoarseness strongly suggesting viral disease.
oneLinePearl: Test children who plausibly have GAS; do not treat the appearance of the tonsils.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society — Group A streptococcal pharyngitis practical guide

title: Childhood Exanthems: Recognize the Pattern, Protect the Dangerous Mimics
bottomLine: Most childhood exanthems are diagnosed from fever timing, morphology, distribution, mucosal findings, immunization/exposure and clinical appearance. The priority is recognizing measles/public-health disease, scarlet fever/GAS, Kawasaki/MIS-C, meningococcemia, severe drug reactions and immunocompromised hosts—not naming every benign viral rash from memory.
recognize: Roseola classically has fever before rash; hand-foot-mouth disease has characteristic acral/oral lesions; varicella has lesions in different stages.
Measles is a high-consequence febrile rash illness requiring immediate infection-control/public-health action when suspected.
differentiate: Blanching viral rash differs from non-blanching petechiae/purpura in an ill child.
Scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease, MIS-C and medication reactions can mimic viral exanthems but have different treatment urgency.
assessment: Assess immunization/travel/exposure, fever timing, toxicity, rash morphology/distribution/blanching, mucosa, conjunctiva, extremities, lymph nodes, medications and immune status.
workup: Typical benign exanthems need little testing; suspected measles/other reportable disease, invasive bacterial infection or inflammatory syndrome needs targeted laboratory/public-health evaluation.
management: Provide supportive care for uncomplicated viral exanthem and disease-specific infection control.
Escalate toxic/purpuric, mucosal blistering, Kawasaki/MIS-C or invasive bacterial patterns.
medicationSafety: Avoid aspirin in routine viral illness; Kawasaki treatment is a separate specialist-guided indication.
Do not attribute mucosal blistering after a new medication to a benign viral rash without evaluating severe cutaneous drug reaction.
counselling: Give isolation/school/daycare and return guidance based on the actual disease rather than a generic 'rash is contagious' rule.
followUp: Reassess persistent fever, evolving systemic findings or diagnostic uncertainty.
examTrap: Calling every febrile rash viral when the child has non-blanching purpura or persistent fever with Kawasaki features.
oneLinePearl: With exanthems, the dangerous question is how sick the child is and which public-health/inflammatory mimics must not be missed.

title: Pediatric Murmurs: Innocent Pattern or Structural Heart Disease?
bottomLine: Most childhood murmurs are innocent, but age, symptoms, oxygenation, pulses and murmur characteristics determine who needs echocardiography/cardiology. A murmur in a cyanotic, poorly feeding, syncopal or growth-faltering child is not an incidental sound.
recognize: Innocent murmurs are typically soft, systolic and occur in an otherwise well child with normal pulses/oxygenation/growth.
Pathologic clues include diastolic/continuous abnormal patterns, harsh/loud murmurs, abnormal S2/click, radiation, cyanosis or abnormal pulses.
differentiate: A normal neonatal pulse-ox screen reduces but does not eliminate congenital heart disease risk.
Fever with a new murmur raises a different differential than a stable lifelong innocent murmur.
assessment: Assess feeding/exercise tolerance, diaphoresis, cyanosis, syncope/chest pain, growth, family sudden-death/cardiomyopathy history, SpO2, four-limb pulse quality and full cardiac exam.
workup: Refer/obtain echocardiography when symptoms or pathologic features are present; routine ECG/CXR/echo is unnecessary for a clearly innocent murmur in a well child.
management: Reassure innocent murmurs without unnecessary activity restriction.
Urgently evaluate cyanosis, heart failure, exertional syncope or critical newborn findings; refer other suspected structural disease appropriately.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe endocarditis prophylaxis solely because a murmur exists; prophylaxis depends on defined high-risk cardiac conditions/procedures.
counselling: Explain that a murmur is a sound, not a diagnosis, and most innocent murmurs do not limit activity.
followUp: Track symptoms/growth and referral results; re-evaluate if the murmur or clinical pattern changes.
examTrap: Ordering echocardiography for every soft systolic murmur—or reassuring a child with exertional syncope because murmurs are common.
oneLinePearl: The child determines the risk of the murmur, not the murmur alone.

title: Pediatric Orthopedics: Age, Gait, Trauma, and the Hot Joint
bottomLine: Pediatric musculoskeletal complaints must be interpreted by age and development. Most benign limb/gait variants need reassurance, but inability to bear weight, hot joint, significant trauma, night pain/systemic symptoms, neurovascular compromise or age-specific hip pathology needs urgent targeted evaluation.
recognize: Transient synovitis, developmental variants and overuse are common; septic arthritis/osteomyelitis, fracture, SCFE and malignancy are cannot-miss alternatives in the right age/context.
differentiate: A well child with mild post-viral limp differs from a febrile child refusing weight bearing.
Growing pains are bilateral/intermittent/nighttime with normal daytime function/exam and are not a label for persistent focal pain or swelling.
assessment: Assess trauma, fever, pain location including referred hip/knee pain, gait/weight bearing, swelling, range of motion, neurovascular status, systemic symptoms and age/puberty/body habitus.
workup: Use radiographs, ultrasound, CBC/inflammatory markers or advanced imaging when fracture, infection, SCFE, malignancy or other significant pathology is plausible; avoid routine imaging of normal developmental variants.
management: Urgently refer suspected septic joint, SCFE, compartment/neurovascular compromise or unstable fracture.
Treat benign variants/overuse conservatively with activity guidance and reassessment if the trajectory changes.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not be withheld to preserve diagnostic findings; dose by weight and account for renal/GI risk.
counselling: Explain expected developmental variants while providing clear return precautions for pain, limp, swelling or systemic change.
followUp: Persistent limp/pain after an initially benign assessment requires diagnostic reconsideration.
examTrap: Calling a febrile child who refuses to bear weight 'transient synovitis' without excluding septic arthritis.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric orthopedics, inability to bear weight plus fever is infection until appropriately excluded.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society osteoarticular infection guidance
